recentItems.title: New trade corridors emerge in new tariff era, says HSBC Global trade head | The Business | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
HSBC's head of global trade solutions, Vivek Ramachandran says in an era of Donald Trump's tariffs, the world is becoming more interconnected than ever with an increase in bilateral trade deals and new trade corridors emerging.

He joined The Business while visiting Australia, saying the new deals may be a consequence of US tariffs and trade wars or it may be a natural evolution of demand in other markets growing faster than anticipated.

"India just signed a trade agreement with the UK and the same with the EU is underway. The GCC is signing new trade deals," he says.

His assessment comes as the United States and Canada ramp up their tariff war, with Canada retaliating against recent US duties and bans on a variety of Canadian products including alcoholic spirits, dairy goods and motorbikes.

When asked whether middle powers are beginning to form alliances as Canada's prime minister Mark Carney has called for, Mr Ramachandran says so far there's no sign of anything other than bilateral trade deals.

He suggests that could be because the US consumer makes up around 30-35 per cent of global consumption, making it difficult for any company or country to ignore trade opportunities with the US.

As far as Australia's current trading environment is concerned, he says Australia is doing a good job at balancing the needs and demands of trade with two competing superpowers - China and the US.

And he says the two biggest forces reshaping global trade, the AI investment boom and services, have nothing to do with the US military action against Iran, and resulting impact on energy supply.

recentItems.title: Millions in debt racked up through tax and super systems | The Business | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) would be given powers to stop illegal withdrawals of super from self-managed super funds (SMSFs). Perpetrators of financial abuse often set up a joint SMSF, clear money out of the fund illegally, and then leave the victim facing hefty penalties and risk of imprisonment after the money is gone. Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino is unveiling measures aimed at closing the opportunities for financial abuse. He has been considering 61 recommendations made by a parliamentary inquiry into financial abuse. He wants to put greater onus on all financial services providers, including banks, other credit lenders, insurance companies and superannuation funds, to look for signs of financial abuse. Mr Mulino said perpetrators needed to face tougher penalties if they coerced someone into being a company director to rack up tax debts in their name. He is also considering how penalties for tax debts could be waived for victims of financial abuse.

recentItems.title: Back-to-back rate hikes can't be ruled out, says CBA chief economist | The Business | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
Commonwealth Bank's base case is that the RBA will hike in November, but its chief economist says the central bank could move higher in September.  Luke Yeaman says back-to-back hikes at both meetings can't be ruled out.

"At this stage, we think one more interest rate hike should be enough, especially with the housing market coming off so sharply to help slow consumption, slow activity in the economy, and very slowly bring inflation back to target," he says.

Mr Yeaman's comments came one day after RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser told the ABC taming inflation is the Australian central bank's number one problem.

The chief economist, and former Treasury deputy secretary, says another problem making the RBA's job more difficult is the persistently high oil price, with the Middle East conflict driving Brent crude near $US100 a barrel on Wednesday.

Mr Yeaman says if there's a bigger escalation and oil prices rise beyond $US100 a barrel, it will feed into prices back through the economy in coming months and into 2027.

"That would be the thing that could push the RBA to have to go harder," he says.

recentItems.title: Don't mistake progress for success on ending violence, minister warns Australia | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
Tanya Plibersek has tabled the Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commission's annual assessment of how Australia's going in ending violence against women and children.

The minister for social services says while Australia should be proud of the progress it's made, it can't mistake progress for success.

She says Australia has to shift from just responding to violence to dealing with the conditions that cause and exacerbate it.

The minister also told parliament that it means getting support to families before they reach crisis, and delivering on frontline services people depend on.

"If we want violence to become rare, brief and non-recurring as the commissioner states, we must ensure that all areas of government at all levels — social security, education, health, justice — are speaking to each other and pulling in the same direction," Ms Plibersek says.

"Crucially, we must confront the attitudes and behaviours across our communities that still minimise, excuse or allow violence to remain hidden in plain sight."

recentItems.title: Trial begins for men accused of killing Robinson brothers in Mexico | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
A trial has begun for three men accused of murdering two Australian brothers and their American friend in Mexico.

Jesús Gerardo, also known as "El Kekas", Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús are facing a number of charges for the alleged killing of Jake and Callum Robinson, and Jack Carter Rhoad in 2024.

Trial by jury in criminal cases is uncommon in Mexico, where verdicts and sentences are usually decided by a trial magistrate or panels of magistrates. But the trial of the three men is being overseen by a single judge.

Ahead of the trial, a new judge was appointed in a dramatic last-minute change. He appeared remotely because there wasn't enough time to get him to Ensenada to attend court in person.

The trial is expected to run for more than four weeks.
